draft.title: Liveability
card: Liveability is how good a place is to live. It is judged by how well the place meets the everyday needs of the people who live there.

Common measures are housing, transport, safety, services, jobs, things to do, green space and the environment. Services include schools, health care and shops. Things to do include sport, entertainment and recreation.
A place with affordable housing, reliable public transport, low crime and clean air is likely to be seen as more liveable.
Liveability is judged across the measures together, and a place can be strong on some and weak on others. People may rate the same place differently, because they value different things.
draft.remember: Liveability is how well a place meets residents' daily needs across several measures.

a.q: Which of these is a measure of how liveable a town is?
opts: How easily residents can reach schools and clinics
How many people were born in the city last year
How much farmland lies beyond the edge of the city
How many tourists visit the city each year
a.why: Access to schools and clinics is part of services, which shape residents' daily lives, so it is a measure of liveability. Tourist numbers describe visitors, not how well the place meets the needs of the people who live there.
a.clue: Think about what matters to people living there each day.

b.q: Dara moves to a suburb with cheap rent, low crime and a large park. The nearest train station is 40 minutes away and there is no clinic. How liveable is it overall?
opts: Mixed, as some measures are strong and others are weak
High, because cheap rent is the main measure of liveability
Low, because one weak measure makes a suburb unliveable
Unknown, because liveability cannot be judged by measures
b.why: Housing, safety and green space look strong, while transport and services look weak. Liveability is judged across several measures together, so the result is mixed. It is wrong to say one measure alone decides it, in either direction.
b.clue: Can one detail decide liveability on its own?

a.best: How easily residents can reach schools and clinics

b.best: Mixed, as some measures are strong and others are weak

proposal.title: What liveability means
card: Liveability is how well a place meets people's needs for a good life. A highly liveable place lets people live safely and comfortably.
These needs include safety, services, jobs, a clean environment and things to do. Services are things like schools, health care, shops and public transport.
Jobs let people earn an income close to home. Things to do include sport, parks, entertainment and community events.
A place can meet some needs well and others poorly. To judge how liveable it is, look at all of these needs together.
proposal.remember: A liveable place meets many needs for a good life, not just one.

a.q: Which change would make a town more liveable for its residents?
opts: A new health clinic opens in the town
The town's only bus route is cut
Crime rises in the town centre
Smoke from a factory drifts over the town
a.why: A clinic adds a service that residents need, so the town meets more of their needs. Cutting the bus route removes a service, and rising crime or smoke make the town less safe or less clean, so each lowers liveability.
a.clue: Which change helps meet a need, rather than taking one away?

b.q: Dara's suburb has low crime, a large park and local jobs. It has no bus service and no clinic. How liveable is it overall?
opts: Mixed, as it meets some needs well and others poorly
High, because safety is the only need that really counts
Low, because one unmet need makes a place unliveable
Unknown, because liveability depends only on the shops
b.why: Safety, things to do and jobs are well met, but transport and health care are missing. Liveability looks at all the needs together, so the result is mixed. Saying one need alone decides it, in either direction, ignores the rest.
b.clue: Can one need decide liveability on its own?
